Persist pooled PHP writes to saved sites (#4260)

## What

Persist filesystem changes made by pooled PHP instances to autosaved
Playground sites after the request completes.

This supersedes #4240 with the architecture Brandon proposed: PROXYFS
propagates replica request completion to the filesystem owner, while the
OPFS journal remains solely responsible for deciding when to flush.

## Root cause

Playground web uses a pool of PHP instances. Secondary instances access
shared paths through PROXYFS backed by the primary PHP instance. Their
writes are captured by the primary instance's OPFS journal, but
`request.end` is emitted only by the secondary instance. The primary
journal therefore has no completion signal for the proxied request, and
recent changes can remain queued in memory instead of reaching OPFS.

## Deterministic regression proof

The Chromium test exercises the original saved-site symptom instead of
asserting any event or flush machinery introduced by this PR:

- It writes a unique sentinel outside the proxied mounts, so only the
primary PHP runtime can see it.
- The first request creates a file barrier and remains blocked; the
second request then creates its own barrier and remains blocked. The
test observes each barrier instead of sleeping to guess when either
request started, then overwrites the same file to release that request.
- The test releases and fully awaits the first request before allowing
the second request to write the marker, eliminating a later primary
`request.end` that could accidentally flush it.
- The completed responses prove the requests ran on `primary` and
`secondary`, respectively.
- A public `readFileAsText()` call proves the marker reached the shared
live VFS, then an independent read of the autosaved site's real OPFS
directory checks the persisted bytes.

At red SHA
[`4a5116926`](https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-playground/commit/4a5116926dbfbd51d9b733b463ac97b3f5557072),
the PR contained only this test. The Chromium storage job reached the
final OPFS assertion on all four attempts and consistently received
`undefined` instead of the marker contents; all other 60 tests passed.
See the [expected failed CI
job](https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-playground/actions/runs/31738099889/job/94574529357).

The regression test at the fixed SHA is byte-for-byte identical to the
red version.

## Implementation

- `proxyFileSystem()` forwards a replica's `request.end` as
`proxyfs.request.end` on the filesystem owner.
- `journalFSEventsToOpfs()` handles that lifecycle event through its
existing single-flight background flush, alongside direct `request.end`
and `filesystem.write` triggers.
- Journal teardown removes the new listener with its existing listeners.

This keeps pool-specific behavior out of Playground's worker and keeps
OPFS flush ownership inside the journaling abstraction. It does not
change export code or introduce an export lock.

## Validation

- Red CI: [Chromium storage
job](https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-playground/actions/runs/31738099889/job/94574529357)
— the regression test alone fails at the persisted-bytes assertion on
all four attempts.
- Local green: universal tests 184 passed / 4 skipped; web tests 60
passed; website rerun 377 passed; affected typechecks and lints passed.
- Green CI: [full CI
run](https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-playground/actions/runs/31740060392)
and [Chromium storage
job](https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-playground/actions/runs/31740060392/job/94581003107)
passed on fixed SHA
[`b9013b91e`](https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-playground/commit/b9013b91e0d98e7783aaca3a3c6360ddde9822df).

[Website] Auto-prepend PHP scripts before snippet execution (#4262)

Adds two independent `<php-snippet>` options:

- `auto-prepend-script` points to an inert, complete PHP script that
runs before every execution, mirroring PHP's `auto_prepend_file`
directive.
- `implicit-php-open-tag` adds a PHP opening tag before visible source
that omits it.

```html
<script id="load-wordpress" type="application/x-php">
<?php require_once '/wordpress/wp-load.php';
</script>

<php-snippet
    name="site-title.php"
    auto-prepend-script="#load-wordpress"
    implicit-php-open-tag
>
    <script type="application/x-php">
echo get_bloginfo( 'name' );
    </script>
</php-snippet>
```

`implicit-php-open-tag` also works without hidden setup:

```html
<php-snippet name="sum.php" implicit-php-open-tag>
    <script type="application/x-php">
echo array_sum( [ 10, 20, 12 ] );
    </script>
</php-snippet>
```

An auto-prepended script also works when the visible snippet includes
its own opening tag:

```html
<php-snippet name="site-title.php" auto-prepend-script="#load-wordpress">
    <script type="application/x-php">
<?php
echo get_bloginfo( 'name' );
    </script>
</php-snippet>
```

The auto-prepended script and snippet remain separate PHP files. Each
complete file owns its opening tag; `implicit-php-open-tag` adds an
opener only to visible source that omits it. The snippet keeps the
filename from `name`, so PHP diagnostics map back to the displayed code.
Per-request setup also lets snippets with different setup code share a
runtime without leaking it into later runs.

Snippets using neither option keep the existing eval path.

Closes #4261.

## Testing

Open the PHP snippet E2E fixture. Run a snippet with
`auto-prepend-script` and `implicit-php-open-tag`, then one with only
`implicit-php-open-tag`. Confirm only the first can call WordPress, both
report their displayed first line, and only one runtime iframe is
created.

[CI] Republish packages missing after a partial NPM release (#4270)

## Why this change is needed

The scheduled release of 3.1.50 published 38 of 40 packages:
`@php-wasm/web-5-2` and `@php-wasm/web-7-4` failed with
`TLOG_CREATE_ENTRY_ERROR (409)` and stayed at 3.1.49 on npm, while
`@php-wasm/web@3.1.50` pinned both at 3.1.50. Every install resolving
`@php-wasm/web@3.1.50` failed until the two packages were republished by
hand three days later. The same failure previously hit
`@php-wasm/node-polyfills@3.0.37` (#3090). Lerna keeps publishing after
an individual package fails and only exits 1 at the end, so a partial
release leaves npm with unsatisfiable dependencies and nothing repairs
it.

## What this changes

Adds a `Republish missing packages` step, gated on the publish step
itself failing (`failure() && steps.publish.conclusion == 'failure'`) so
earlier failures like checkout or build do not trigger it. It calls
`lerna publish from-package`, which inspects each `package.json` and
publishes only the versions absent from the registry — exactly the
packages that failed, through the same Lerna pipeline and the
already-built dist output. The job still fails, so a partial release
stays visible, but npm is repaired within the same run.

If Lerna fails before the version bump, the `package.json` files still
hold the previous, fully published versions, so `from-package` is a
no-op and nothing wrong gets published.

[CI] Label PRs from git diff instead of the pulls.listFiles API (#4290)

## Why

The **Auto-label PRs** workflow is a required check, and it fails on any
PR that changes a lot of binary data — most notably PRs that recompile
the PHP.wasm builds — which then **blocks the merge** even though the
real CI is green.

The cause: both of the workflow's jobs listed a PR's changed files from
GitHub's `pulls.listFiles` API (the `paths` job via `actions/labeler`,
the `package-and-type` job directly). That makes GitHub generate the
**full PR diff**, and on a PR with hundreds of MB of changed binaries it
gives up:

```
HttpError: Server Error: Sorry, this diff is taking too long to generate: {"code":"not_available"}
```

Retrying doesn't help — for a large PR the diff is consistently too big
to generate. #3812 added a catch to the `package-and-type` job, but it
only **skips** labeling on those PRs (and, because the early `return`
sits above the title logic, it even drops the title-derived `[Type]`
label, which needs no file data at all). `actions/labeler`'s internal
`listFiles` call can't be wrapped.

## What

List the changed files with **`git diff` instead of `listFiles`**. `git
diff` compares tree object hashes and never serializes blob content, so
it's **instant regardless of PR size** — the thing that was timing out
is gone — and it lets both label sets actually **succeed** on
binary-heavy PRs instead of being skipped.

Just as important: this **consolidates the two divergent labeling flows
into one**. There used to be `actions/labeler` + a separate
`github-script` job; now a **single `git diff --numstat`** feeds every
label set, computed by small unit-tested modules and posted once:

- **`[Aspect]`/`[Focus]`/`[Feature]`/`[Type] Documentation`** — path
globs (`match-path-labels.mjs`).
- **`[Package][...]`** — top-3 packages by lines changed, file count as
tiebreaker (`rank-package-labels.mjs`).
- **`[Type]`** — the PR title's conventional-commit prefix
(`match-type-label.mjs`).

```
packages/meta/src/pr-labels/label-rules.mjs            # all rule sets, one place
packages/meta/src/pr-labels/match-path-labels.mjs      (+ .test.mjs)
packages/meta/src/pr-labels/rank-package-labels.mjs    (+ .test.mjs)
packages/meta/src/pr-labels/match-type-label.mjs       (+ .test.mjs)
packages/meta/src/pr-labels/git-numstat.mjs            (+ .test.mjs)
packages/meta/bin/label-pr.mjs                         # thin git + API runner
```

Run the tests locally (32 cases):
```
node --test packages/meta/src/pr-labels/*.test.mjs
```
They also run in CI — a dedicated `test-pr-labels` job runs this suite
on every PR. (`packages/meta` isn't an nx project, so `nx affected
--target=test` wouldn't otherwise cover them.)

The **rule sets live in one module**: `label-rules.mjs` holds all three
(`PATH_LABEL_RULES`, `PACKAGE_RULES`, `TYPE_RULES`) so a maintainer can
read and adjust everything that drives labeling in one place; each
matcher imports and defaults to its set. Since `actions/labeler` is
gone, nothing else consumed `.github/labeler.yml`, so its path globs
moved here too and **`.github/labeler.yml` is removed** — no YAML
parsing anywhere. The runner reads nothing on its own — no config file,
no event payload; it gets the PR facts (number, base SHA, title) via
env.

## Notes

- `git diff` runs **no PR code** (only reads paths and line counts), so
reading the fork head stays safe under `pull_request_target`. The PR
title is passed as an **env var** (not interpolated into a shell
command), so an attacker-controlled title can't inject.
- Glob matching uses minimatch with `{ dot: true }` — **identical to
`actions/labeler` v5** — so path labels are unchanged from before.
- Actions stay **pinned to commit SHAs** (`checkout` added as `v4.2.2`).
The label modules' runtime dependencies are declared in
`packages/meta/src/pr-labels/package.json` with a committed lockfile and
installed via `npm ci --prefix` scoped to that dir — normal declared
dependencies, not an ad-hoc install, and they don't touch the repo's
workspaces.
- For a pure-binary PR, `numstat` reports `-` for binaries (counted as 0
lines), so package ranking falls to the file-count tiebreaker — fine,
and strictly better than today's "no labels at all."
- **Robust diff** (`git-numstat.mjs` owns the invocation): `git diff
--numstat -z --no-renames`. `-z` gives verbatim, NUL-terminated paths,
so a file with a tab / non-ASCII name still matches its prefix/glob;
`--no-renames` avoids git's brace-compressed rename paths; a 64 MiB
`maxBuffer` prevents `ENOBUFS` on a very large diff. The dependency
install uses `--ignore-scripts`, and `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` is passed
explicitly.
- **Breaking-change titles**: `[Type]` now recognizes

CI: Slim down the Auto-label PR checkout to the minimum needed (#4291)

## Why

The Auto-label workflow added in #4290 checks out with `fetch-depth: 0`.
That's a full-history clone that downloads **every blob across all of
history** — and this repo commits large PHP.wasm and WordPress binaries
— plus `actions/checkout` then materializes the **entire HEAD working
tree** (more big binaries) on disk. The job never reads any of that.

All the job actually does with git is:
1. `git fetch` the PR head, and
2. `git diff --numstat -z --no-renames base...head` (three-dot, in
`packages/meta/src/pr-labels/git-numstat.mjs`).

That diff runs entirely off the object database (commit/tree/blob OIDs).
Its only real needs are the **merge-base** of base and head, and the
**blobs of the files that actually changed**. Full history and a full
working tree are far more than that.

## What

Keep `fetch-depth: 0` but add two filters so the checkout fetches the
minimum:

- `filter: blob:none` — blobless partial clone. Fetches the full commit
+ tree graph (still required so the merge-base is present) but **no
historical blobs**; git lazily fetches only the changed blobs the diff
reads.
- `sparse-checkout: packages/meta` — materialize only the directory
whose scripts the job runs (`bin/label-pr.mjs`, `src/pr-labels/*`, and
the `npm ci` lockfile), so checkout doesn't pull HEAD's big binaries
onto disk either.

`fetch-depth: 0` stays: a stale PR's merge-base can be arbitrarily far
back, so a fixed shallow depth would risk breaking the three-dot diff.

### Change detection is unaffected

`sparse-checkout` only limits what's written to the **working tree** —
it has no effect on `git diff`, which compares named commits via the
object DB. Whole-repo labeling still works exactly as before; the job
just stops downloading binaries it never opens.

Await php.ini writes during boot (#4265)

## Why

This PR is one of three that enable recording Xdebug traces and profiles
from Playground. Recording requires php.ini entries such as
`xdebug.mode` to be set before PHP serves its first request: this PR
makes the boot-time php.ini writes land before that request, #4280 adds
a generic way to set entries — a target path on `setPhpIniEntries()` and
a `--php-ini` CLI flag — and #4281 documents the resulting trace and
profile workflow.

## Root cause

`bootRequestHandler()` called `setPhpIniEntries()` without awaiting it.
That function awaits `php.readFileAsText()` before writing, so it
returns at the await point and the write to `php.ini` lands in a later
microtask.

`applyLegacyPhpIniOverrides()` ran next and merged the legacy
network-disable list into the same file. On legacy PHP it could read
`php.ini` before the `phpIniEntries` write had landed, and the late
write then overwrote `disable_functions`, `allow_url_fopen`, and
`date.timezone`. `applyLegacyPhpIniOverrides()` had the same defect
internally: it called `setPhpIniEntries()` without awaiting and returned
`void`.

## What this changes

`createPhp()` in `boot.ts` awaits both `setPhpIniEntries()` and
`applyLegacyPhpIniOverrides()`. `applyLegacyPhpIniOverrides()` becomes
`async`, returns `Promise<void>`, and awaits its own write.

This is not a breaking change. `applyLegacyPhpIniOverrides()` is not
re-exported from `@wp-playground/wordpress` and `bootRequestHandler()`
is its only caller.

## Testing

- `npx nx test playground-wordpress` — 136 passed.
- `npx nx run playground-cli:test-playground-cli
--testFiles=run-cli.spec.ts` — 97 passed.

[Website] Escape and sandbox the Blueprint Builder error iframe (#4329)

## What

The Blueprint Builder runs the Blueprint from the URL fragment on load.
When a Blueprint fails v2 schema validation, the error message quotes
the offending property name — which comes from the fragment and is
therefore untrusted text — and `showError()` interpolated it straight
into the error iframe's `srcdoc`. That iframe had no `sandbox`, so the
`srcdoc` document inherited the Playground origin and any markup in the
message ran as same-origin script.

## Fix

Two independent defenses, either of which stops it:

1. **Escape the message and render it in a `<pre>`** (`builder.ts`) —
untrusted text reaches the document as text, not markup. This is the
primary fix.
2. **`sandbox=""` on the error iframe** (`builder.html`) — it only ever
shows text, so it needs neither script nor origin access. Defense in
depth.

## Tests

Adds `builder-error-xss.spec.ts`, which fails on the vulnerable code:

- Loads a Blueprint whose property name is an `onerror` payload and
asserts it does **not** execute and that the rendered `srcdoc` is
escaped.
- Asserts the error iframe keeps its `sandbox`.

Verified the spec passes with the fix and fails without it (both
assertions), and `nx lint` / `nx typecheck` for `playground-website` are
clean.

## Notes

- The error-escaping helper duplicates a local `escapeHtml` in
`personal-wp`; not consolidated here since these are different packages
and `builder.ts` is a standalone `@ts-nocheck` browser script. Flagging
in case a shared util is preferred as separate cleanup.

fix(meta): changelog: prevent Markdown/<HTML/> injection via PR titles (#4333)

## What

Escape untrusted PR titles before they are interpolated into the
generated changelog, in two independent layers, and gate changelog
generation on tests. PR titles are attacker-controllable — a public
author can rename their own PR *after* it is merged, and the weekly
changelog job re-queries the live title, commits it to `trunk`, and
deploys it to the `wordpress.github.io/wordpress-playground` docs
origin.

## Escaping (two layers)

- `escapeMarkdown` backslash-escapes CommonMark's ASCII-punctuation set
(links, images, emphasis, headings, etc.). Replaces the old
`escapeHtmlForMarkdown`, which used `String.prototype.replace('<', …)` —
only the **first** occurrence — and only handled angle brackets, so
`<decoy> <iframe …>` left the second tag raw (still visible in the
committed changelog, e.g. the `#3536` entry) and Markdown link/image
injection was never addressed.
- `escapeHtml` entity-encodes `<`, `>`, `&` as a **second, independent
layer**, so a raw tag cannot form even if the Markdown processor
mishandles backslash escapes.

The two layers are **partitioned** (`escapeHtml` owns `< > &`,
`escapeMarkdown` owns the rest) — escaping the same character with both
corrupts the rendered output. `escapeMarkdown` runs first so it doesn't
backslash-mangle `escapeHtml`'s `&`/`<` entities (documented
inline where the order is set). Docusaurus 3.9.2 renders this doc as
CommonMark (`mdx.format: md`) via micromark + remark-gfm; both layers
hold under GFM.

## Feature-prefix cleanup fix

`escapeMarkdown` escapes `[`, `-`, and `:`, which defeated
`getFeatureEntry`'s prefix-cleanup regexes (they matched raw delimiters
on the already-escaped entry). Cleanup now runs on the **raw title
before escaping**, so redundant `[Feature - …]` / `Feature: ` prefixes
are stripped again. (Addresses the CodeRabbit review finding.)

## Tests + CI

`packages/meta` is not an nx project, so its tests are outside `nx
affected --target=test`. Two places now run them:
- **`test-changelog`** job in `ci.yml` — runs on every PR.
- **`update-changelog.yml`** — a gate step runs the spec **before** the
changelog is generated/committed/deployed at release time.

`changelog.spec.ts` covers: the two-tag first-occurrence regression,
`escapeMarkdown` metacharacter escaping, `escapeHtml` entity-encoding
(ampersand-first), the two-layer wiring via `getNormalizedTitle`, the
feature-prefix cleanup (and that it still escapes hostile titles), and a
**"Changelog can be safely generated from hostile PR titles"**
end-to-end check over the real entry generators.

## Breaking changes

None.

[CI] Restore the working tree before republishing missing packages (#4349)

## Motivation for the change, related issues

The 3.1.55 release repeated the #4269 failure: a transient OIDC 503 made
`@php-wasm/node-8-1` fail to publish, and `@php-wasm/node@3.1.55` pinned
it at a version absent from npm. The `Republish missing packages` step
added in #4270 triggered but exited immediately with `EUNCOMMIT`: a
failed `lerna publish` leaves the working tree dirty (unrestored
`package.json` edits and regenerated build files), and `lerna publish
from-package` refuses to run on a dirty tree. The safety net can never
fire in the exact situation it was built for. See the failed run:
https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-playground/actions/runs/35582526148

## Implementation details

The step now runs `git checkout -- .` before `lerna publish
from-package`. On trunk the version bump commit is at HEAD when the step
runs, so the restore keeps the bumped versions and `from-package`
publishes exactly the packages missing from the registry. On non-trunk
runs (`--no-push --no-git-tag-version`) the bump is never committed, so
the restore reverts it and `from-package` publishes nothing — the same
inert-but-safe behavior as today.

## Testing Instructions (or ideally a Blueprint)

This step only runs when a publish partially fails, so it cannot be
exercised on demand. The failed 3.1.55 run shows the exact `EUNCOMMIT`
state this fixes: every listed uncommitted file is restorable from HEAD,
and `git describe` already resolved to the `v3.1.55` tag
(`v3.1.55-0-g4a5af3fd0-dirty`), confirming the restore lands on the
bumped versions.

[CORS Proxy] Support range requests from browsers (#4362)

## Motivation for the change, related issues

Range requests are a standard part of HTTP, and the CORS proxy should
support them for any client. Resumable downloads, media seeking, and
reading parts of large files all depend on them.

This PR was prompted by a Kandelo need. Kandelo reads ZIP archive
indexes through the CORS proxy without downloading whole archives. That
takes three or four small range reads: the end-of-central-directory
record via a suffix range, then the central directory, then individual
members.

The proxy already forwarded `Range` and relayed `206`, but browsers
could not use it:

- Preflight did not allow `Range`. Browsers only safelist simple
`bytes=N-M` ranges, so suffix ranges like `bytes=-22` were blocked.
- `Content-Range`, `Accept-Ranges`, and `ETag` are not CORS-safelisted
response headers, so scripts could not read them.

Running requests against the production deployment also showed that the
WP Cloud front end **strips `Range` and `If-Range`** before the request
reaches PHP. It also rewrites `Accept-Encoding` to `gzip, br`. Custom
headers pass through untouched, and responses (`206`, `416`,
`Content-Range`, `ETag`) come back intact.

**Merge order:** this PR, then #4364, then #4365. #4364 is stacked on
this PR, and #4365 is stacked on #4364.

## Implementation details

- Add `Range` to `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`.
- Add `Content-Range`, `Accept-Ranges`, and `ETag` to
`Access-Control-Expose-Headers`. `Last-Modified` is already safelisted.
- When the outgoing request has a range, send `Accept-Encoding:
identity` to the target so byte offsets refer to the unencoded body.
Browsers already do this for `Range` requests per the Fetch spec, but
the front end overwrites the value.
- **Workaround:** clients may send `X-Cors-Proxy-Range`, which the proxy
forwards to the target as `Range`. The internal header is never
forwarded. The code carries a `WORKAROUND:` comment, and the README has
a note, both listing what to remove once `Range` reaches PHP on WP
Cloud. I confirmed that production's front end lets this header through.
- Size cap: `MAX_RESPONSE_SIZE` is still checked against the response's
`Content-Length`, which on a `206` is the slice length. A small read of
a multi-GiB file therefore works, and a test guards against "fixing"
this by parsing the total out of `Content-Range`. An inline comment now
documents an existing limitation: the cap is only enforced against a
declared `Content-Length`, so responses without one, such as chunked
responses, stream through at any size. Range requests make such
responses easier to reach, but enforcing a hard limit is out of scope
here.
- No range parsing or multi-range support was added. `If-Range` is not
allowed.
- `Range` takes priority over `X-Cors-Proxy-Range`. Clients may send
both with the same value, so they keep working once the workaround is
removed; the proxy then forwards `Range` unchanged. If the two disagree,
the proxy responds with `400 Bad Request` rather than silently ignore
one.
- An empty `X-Cors-Proxy-Range` is ignored. Otherwise curl would treat
the resulting empty `Range` header as a removal and drop the client's
real `Range`.
- If the target fails after the proxy has started sending its response,
the proxy now ends the response instead of appending a "Bad Gateway"
message to the body. Previously a truncated `206` could carry that text
as if it were file bytes. If the target fails before the proxy has sent
anything, for example right after its headers, the proxy still returns
`502`. The proxy does not relay `Content-Length`, so clients can detect
a short `206` by comparing the body length with `Content-Range`.
- When the proxy replaces the target's response with its own `413` or
`502`, it removes every header relayed from the target, e.g.
`Content-Range`, `Location`, or `Transfer-Encoding`, since they describe
a response that never arrived. It then restores a snapshot of the
headers queued before the target was contacted: the CORS headers,
`Cache-Control: no-cache`, and any set by the deployment in
`cors-proxy-config.php` or an `auto_prepend_file`. `Cache-Control` is
now set before that snapshot instead of when the target's status
arrives.

**Edge caching:** ranged responses must never be stored by the WP Cloud
edge cache. Every range of a file shares one proxy URL, so a cached
slice could be served for another range, and many distinct slices would
add cache noise.

- Edge caching has been disabled for all proxy responses since #1930
(for #1920). This PR leaves that unchanged.
- WP Cloud's edge cache does not store responses with `Cache-Control:
no-cache`. The proxy sends that header on every response it relays from
a target and never relays the target's own `Cache-Control`.
- The edge also bypasses its cache for any request with an `Origin`
header. Since browsers send `Origin` on every cross-origin request,
re-enabling edge caching for browser traffic would first need a platform
change.
- I verified this against production: responses, including `206`s, are
not stored because of the proxy's `Cache-Control` header.
- The e2e tests now assert this header on `206` and `416` responses. I
confirmed they fail when the header is removed.

**Test harness fixes:**

- The e2e script could not start its servers where `php` is not on the
fallback system path, such as Homebrew PHP on macOS: `proc_open`
replaced the whole environment, dropping `PATH`. It now uses
`PHP_BINARY` and inherits the parent environment.
- `test.sh`, which the `test` target runs, now runs the e2e script after
PHPUnit. Previously nothing ran it.
- Removed the no-op `curl_close()` calls, which emit deprecation
warnings on PHP 8.5.

**Note for reviewers:** because `test.sh` now runs the e2e script, CI's
`nx affected --target=test` will run it when this package changes. It
needs PHP's `curl` and `sockets` extensions, which should be available
on the Ubuntu runners.

## Testing Instructions (or ideally a Blueprint)

```bash
cd packages/playground/php-cors-proxy
bash test.sh
```

Expect PHPUnit to pass, followed by `All 44 assertions passed.` from the
e2e script.

The new e2e tests cover:

- preflight allowing `Range` and `X-Cors-Proxy-Range`;
- a suffix range returning `206` with the right bytes, `Content-Range`,
and exposed headers;
- an unsatisfiable range relaying `416` with `Content-Range: bytes
*/<total>`;
- `206` and `416` responses carrying `Cache-Control: no-cache` so the
edge cache does not store them;
- a small range of a 4 GiB file passing the size cap, and an oversized
slice rejected with `413`;
- the target receiving `Range` and `Accept-Encoding: identity`;
- `X-Cors-Proxy-Range` being forwarded as `Range` and not forwarded
itself;
- `Range` and `X-Cors-Proxy-Range` together: an empty
`X-Cors-Proxy-Range` doesn't drop `Range`, matching values forward one
`Range`, and disagreeing values get `400`;
- a target failing mid-body without an error message being appended, and
a target failing before its body getting `502`;
- the `413` and `502` responses carrying none of the target's headers
while keeping the proxy's own and a header set by the deployment.

The PHPUnit tests use `@dataProvider` annotations, which PHPUnit 13 no
longer supports. I ran them with PHPUnit 9.

After deployment:

[CORS Proxy] Don't relay server-control response headers (#4364)

## Motivation for the change, related issues

The CORS proxy relays most response headers from the target. Some
response headers are instructions to the web server or CDN in front of
PHP rather than to the client:

- nginx performs an internal redirect when PHP sends `X-Accel-Redirect`,
and reads the `X-Accel-*` family for caching, buffering, and rate
limiting.
- Apache with `mod_xsendfile` and lighttpd serve the file named by
`X-Sendfile`, `X-Sendfile-Temporary`, `X-Sendfile2`, or
`X-Lighttpd-Send-File`.
- CGI and FastCGI servers take the response status from a `Status`
header.
- LiteSpeed acts on `X-LiteSpeed-*` headers.
- CDNs read `Surrogate-Control`, `CDN-Cache-Control`, CDN-specific
variants such as `Cloudflare-CDN-Cache-Control`, and Akamai's
`Edge-Control`. A CDN obeys these over `Cache-Control`, so relaying one
would override the proxy's `Cache-Control: no-cache`.

Because the proxy relayed these like any other header, a target could
send instructions to the server hosting the proxy. The proxy should
never do that on a target's behalf.

**Merge order:** this PR, then #4365, which is stacked on it. #4362,
which made the e2e tests runnable, has merged, and this PR is now based
on `trunk`.

## Implementation details

- Add `is_server_control_response_header()` to
`cors-proxy-functions.php`. It matches, case-insensitively:
  - the `X-Accel-` and `X-LiteSpeed-` prefixes;
- `CDN-Cache-Control` and any name ending in `-CDN-Cache-Control`,
following RFC 9213's naming for CDN-specific variants;
- `X-Sendfile`, `X-Sendfile-Temporary`, `X-Sendfile2`,
`X-Lighttpd-Send-File`, `Surrogate-Control`, `Edge-Control`, and
`Status`.
- The response header callback in `cors-proxy.php` drops matching
headers instead of relaying them.

## Testing Instructions (or ideally a Blueprint)

```bash
cd packages/playground/php-cors-proxy
bash test.sh
```

Expect PHPUnit to pass, followed by `All 48 assertions passed.` from the
e2e script.

- `ProxyFunctionsTests::testIsServerControlResponseHeader` covers the
matching rules: prefixes, the CDN suffix, exact names,
case-insensitivity, and look-alike names that must still be relayed,
such as `X-Accelerated-By` and `CDN-Cache-Control-Extension`.
- e2e Test 14 uses a target that sends `X-Accel-Redirect`, `X-Sendfile`,
and `Surrogate-Control` alongside an ordinary `Content-Type`. It checks
that only `Content-Type` is relayed. I confirmed it fails when the
proxy's check is removed.

[CORS Proxy] Support HEAD and relay Content-Length for non-chunked responses (#4365)

## Motivation for the change, related issues

The CORS proxy has not relayed the target's `Content-Length` since
#2077. That PR restructured the response header callback to support
chunked responses, and every special-cased header gained an early
return. #2077 does not discuss dropping `Content-Length`, and the proxy
relayed it before that. Without it:

- Clients can't detect a response cut short by a target failure. The
body just ends early.
- Full responses carry no size. Playground's blueprint download progress
falls back to a 5MB estimate, for example.
- `HEAD` would be useless even if allowed. The proxy rejects it with 405
today.

`HEAD` plus `Content-Length` is the usual way for a client to learn a
file's size before reading ranges, e.g. to locate a ZIP archive's
central directory.

This PR builds on #4362, which added range request support and runs the
e2e tests from `test.sh`, and #4364, which stops relaying server-control
headers. Both have merged, and this PR is based on `trunk`.

## Implementation details

- **Relay `Content-Length` for fixed-length responses.** The header
callback holds the value and emits it when the header block ends, but
only if the response has no `Transfer-Encoding`. RFC 9112 §6.3 says
`Transfer-Encoding` overrides `Content-Length`, and headers can arrive
in either order. The held value resets for each header block, e.g. after
a `100 Continue`, and only digit-only values are relayed.
- Chunked responses are unchanged and still relayed as chunks.
- **Support `HEAD`.** Accept it in the method check, list it in `Allow`
and `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, and set `CURLOPT_NOBODY` so curl
doesn't wait for the announced body. `HEAD` is a CORS-safelisted method,
and `Content-Length` is a safelisted response header, so browsers need
no preflight or exposure for this.
- `HEAD` also asks the target for `Accept-Encoding: identity`, as ranged
requests do. Clients use the `HEAD` size to compute range offsets, so it
must describe the same unencoded bytes the ranges address.
- The response size cap limits relayed bodies, so it no longer applies
to `HEAD`. A `HEAD` on a multi-GiB file returns its size instead of
`413`.
- When the proxy replaces a response with its own `413` or `502`, the
relayed `Content-Length` is removed with the rest of the target's
headers, and the held value is cleared.
- **Fix interim 1xx responses (existing bug).** The proxy took its
status from the first status line curl reported and relayed every header
block. A target that sent `103 Early Hints` or `100 Continue` before its
final response made the proxy answer with that interim status and
headers, followed by the final body, which clients reject. The proxy now
sets its status from the final status line and skips interim header
blocks entirely. A `101 Switching Protocols` isn't skipped: the proxy
can't relay another protocol, so it answers with `502` instead of
presenting the other protocol's bytes as a response body.
- The request body size check now applies only to `POST`, the only
accepted method with a body. Previously any non-`GET` method read
`$_SERVER['CONTENT_LENGTH']`.

**Effects inside Playground:** PHP.wasm's outbound HTTP
(`tcp-over-fetch-websocket.ts`) strips `Content-Length` before handing
responses to PHP, so PHP sees no difference there. `HEAD` requests from
PHP that go through the proxy, e.g. `wp_remote_head()`, now succeed
instead of getting `405`. When the client receives the target's
`Content-Length`, a proxied body cut short now makes `fetch()` fail
instead of returning short data. That doesn't hold for chunked
responses, or when a server in front of PHP compresses the response and
drops `Content-Length`; the README says so. Blueprint resource downloads
and URL-based file reading gain real sizes for progress. When a target
compresses a response, `Content-Length` is the compressed size, so a
download step's progress can show complete before the download ends.
That's cosmetic, since the overall operation can't finish early, and it
already happens with the 5MB fallback.

## Testing Instructions (or ideally a Blueprint)

```bash
cd packages/playground/php-cors-proxy
bash test.sh
```

Expect PHPUnit to pass, followed by `All 66 assertions passed.` from the
e2e script. New and updated e2e tests:

- A fixed-length response relays `Content-Length`.
- A chunked response relays `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` but not
`Content-Length`, even when the target sends `Content-Length` before
`Transfer-Encoding: chunked`. A small raw-socket server,
`tests/e2e/raw-upstream-server.php`, produces that response, because
PHP's built-in server can't send chunked responses. I confirmed this
test fails if `Content-Length` is relayed as soon as it arrives, or
without the chunked check.
- `HEAD` on a 4 GiB file returns `200` with `Content-Length:
4294967296`, and `HEAD` asks the target for `Accept-Encoding: identity`.
- A target that sends `103 Early Hints` before its `200` produces a
`200` response with the final body and without the interim `Link`
header. The raw server also produces this response, and a `101 Switching
Protocols` followed by other bytes, which gets a `502` with only the
proxy's headers.
- A target that fails mid-body now gives the client an
incomplete-response error (`CURLE_PARTIAL_FILE`) instead of a
complete-looking short body. The test also checks that the partial body
holds only the target's bytes; the test helper now captures bodies
through a callback so failed transfers keep what arrived.
